Front: What is a probability space?
Back:
Definition
A probability space is a triple \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\), where \(\Omega\) is a sample space, \(\mathcal F\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\), and \(P:\mathcal F\to[0,1]\) is a probability measure.

Conditions
\(P(\Omega)=1\), and for pairwise disjoint \((A_n)\), \[P\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\right)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(A_n).\]

Front: What is a real-valued random variable on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\)?
Back:
Definition
A measurable function \[X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)).\]

Measurability
Equivalently, \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) and \[X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F\] for every \(B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\).

Front: What is the distribution (or law) of a real-valued random variable \(X\)?
Back:
Definition
The distribution (law) of \(X\) is the pushforward probability measure \(P_X\) on \((\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))\), defined by \[P_X(B):=P\left(X^{-1}(B)\right),\qquad B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).\]

Front: What is the expectation of an integrable real-valued random variable \(X\)?
Back:
Definition
\[\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,dP(\omega).\]

Equivalent law form
\[\mathbb E[X]=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,dP_X(x).\]

Integrability
\[\int_\Omega |X(\omega)|\,dP(\omega)<\infty.\]

Front: What are the basic linearity, constant, and indicator properties of expectation?
Back:
Linearity
For integrable \(X,Y\) and constants \(a,b\), \[\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\mathbb E[X]+b\mathbb E[Y].\]

Constants
\[\mathbb E[c]=c.\]

Indicators
For \(A\in\mathcal F\), \[\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=P(A).\]

Front: What is the precise distinction between a discrete random variable and an absolutely continuous random variable?
Back:
Discrete
Under this program's convention, \(X\) is discrete when \(X(\Omega)\) is finite or countably infinite.

Absolutely continuous
\(X\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) when, for every \(B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\), \[\lambda(B)=0\implies P\left(X^{-1}(B)\right)=0.\] Absolutely continuous random variables have PDFs.

Warning
Singular-continuous and mixed laws also exist.

Front: What is the probability mass function (PMF) of a discrete random variable \(X\)?
Back:
Definition
\[p_X(x):=P\left(X^{-1}(\{x\})\right),\qquad x\in X(\Omega).\]

Recovering probabilities
For every \(B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\), \[P\left(X^{-1}(B)\right)=\sum_{x\in B\cap X(\Omega)}p_X(x).\]

Front: What is the expectation formula for an integrable discrete random variable \(X\)?
Back:
Formula
If \(p_X\) is the PMF of \(X\), then \[\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{x\in X(\Omega)}x\,p_X(x).\]

Integrability
\[\sum_{x\in X(\Omega)}|x|p_X(x)<\infty.\]

Front: What is a probability density function (PDF) of a real-valued random variable \(X\)?
Back:
Definition
A PDF is a Borel-measurable function \[f_X:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\] such that, for every \(B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\), \[P\left(X^{-1}(B)\right)=\int_B f_X(x)\,d\lambda(x).\]

Existence
A PDF exists exactly when the law of \(X\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\).

Front: Give an example of a non-discrete real-valued random variable that has no PDF.
Back:
Construction
On the infinite fair-toss space, let \(B_n(\omega)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate the \(n\)-th toss and define \[X(\omega)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2B_n(\omega)}{3^n}.\]

Why it is not discrete
Its image is the uncountable Cantor set \(C\).

Why it has no PDF
\[P\left(X^{-1}(C)\right)=1,\qquad \lambda(C)=0.\] If a PDF existed, integrating it over \(C\) would have to give both \(1\) and \(0\), a contradiction. Thus \(X\) has a singular-continuous law.

Front: What is the expectation formula when an integrable random variable \(X\) has a PDF \(f_X\)?
Back:
Formula
\[\mathbb E[X]=\int_{\mathbb R}x f_X(x)\,d\lambda(x).\]

Connection
This is the PDF specialization of \[\mathbb E[X]=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,dP_X(x).\]

Front: What is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a real-valued random variable \(X\), and how does it relate to a PMF or PDF?
Back:
Definition
\[F_X(x):=P(X\le x).\] The CDF exists for every real-valued random variable and determines its law.

Discrete case
If \(X\) has PMF \(p_X\), \[F_X(x)=\sum_{k\le x}p_X(k).\]

Absolutely continuous case
If \(X\) has PDF \(f_X\), \[F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f_X(t)\,dt,\] and \(F_X'(x)=f_X(x)\) almost everywhere.

Front: What is the variance of a real-valued random variable \(X\) with finite second moment?
Back:
Definition
Let \(\mu=\mathbb E[X]\). Then \[\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)^2].\]

Equivalent formula
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-(\mathbb E[X])^2.\]

Interpretation
Variance is the expected squared deviation from the mean and is always nonnegative.

Front: What are the main algebraic properties of variance?
Back:
Affine transformation
For constants \(a,b\), \[\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).\]

Non-negativity
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)\ge0.\]

Zero variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=0\iff X=\mathbb E[X]\ \text{almost surely}.\]

Front: What is the standard deviation of \(X\), and how does it transform under affine changes?
Back:
Definition
\[\operatorname{SD}(X):=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.\]

Units
Standard deviation has the same physical units as \(X\).

Affine transformation
\[\operatorname{SD}(aX+b)=|a|\operatorname{SD}(X).\]

Front: Describe the Bernoulli distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), \(0\le p\le1\), represents one binary trial with \(P(X=1)=p\) and \(P(X=0)=1-p\).

Support
\[\{0,1\}.\]

Example/Intuition
Did one particular user click an ad? Encode click as \(1\) and no click as \(0\).

PMF
\[P(X=k)=p^k(1-p)^{1-k},\qquad k\in\{0,1\}.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0,\\1-p,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x\ge1.\end{cases}\]

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=p.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p).\]

Front: Describe the Binomial distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\) counts the number of successes in \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability \(p\).

Support
\[\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.\]

Example/Intuition
Flip a coin 20 times and let \(X\) be the number of heads.

PMF
\[P(X=k)={n\choose k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k},\qquad k=0,\ldots,n.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor x\rfloor}{n\choose k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\] for \(0\le x
Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=np.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p).\]

Front: Describe the Geometric distribution.
Back:
Definition
Using the convention that \(X\) is the trial number of the first success, \(X\sim\operatorname{Geometric}(p)\).

Support
\[\{1,2,3,\ldots\}.\]

Example/Intuition
Make repeated sales calls and let \(X\) be the number of calls until the first sale.

PMF
\[P(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p,\qquad k=1,2,\ldots.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<1,\\1-(1-p)^{\lfloor x\rfloor},&x\ge1.\end{cases}\]

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac1p.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{1-p}{p^2}.\]

Front: Describe the Negative Binomial distribution.
Back:
Definition
Using the convention that \(X\) is the trial number of the \(r\)-th success, \(X\sim\operatorname{NegBin}(r,p)\).

Support
\[\{r,r+1,r+2,\ldots\}.\]

Example/Intuition
Make repeated sales calls and let \(X\) be the number of calls needed to make the 5th sale.

PMF
\[P(X=k)={k-1\choose r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r},\qquad k=r,r+1,\ldots.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\sum_{k=r}^{\lfloor x\rfloor}{k-1\choose r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r}\] for \(x\ge r\), and \(F_X(x)=0\) for \(x
Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac rp.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}.\]

Convention
Some sources count failures before the \(r\)-th success instead of total trials; check the convention.

Front: Describe the Poisson distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), \(\lambda>0\), models a count of events in a fixed interval under the usual Poisson assumptions.

Support
\[\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.\]

Example/Intuition
Let \(X\) be the number of support tickets arriving during one hour.

PMF
\[P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor x\rfloor}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}\] for \(x\ge0\), and \(F_X(x)=0\) for \(x<0\).

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\lambda.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda.\]

Front: Describe the discrete uniform distribution on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Back:
Definition
\(X\) is discrete uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) when each value is equally likely.

Support
\[\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.\]

Example/Intuition
A fair six-sided die is discrete uniform on \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\).

PMF
\[P(X=k)=\frac1n,\qquad k=1,\ldots,n.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<1,\\\frac{\lfloor x\rfloor}{n},&1\le x
Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac{n+1}{2}.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{n^2-1}{12}.\]

Front: Describe the Hypergeometric distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Hypergeometric}(N,K,n)\) counts successes in \(n\) draws without replacement from a population of size \(N\) containing \(K\) successes.

Support
\[\max(0,n-(N-K))\le k\le\min(n,K).\]

Example/Intuition
A box has 100 parts, 10 defective; sample 20 without replacement and let \(X\) be the number of defectives selected.

PMF
\[P(X=k)=\frac{{K\choose k}{N-K\choose n-k}}{{N\choose n}}.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\sum_{\substack{k\le\lfloor x\rfloor\\k\text{ feasible}}}\frac{{K\choose k}{N-K\choose n-k}}{{N\choose n}}.\]

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=n\frac KN.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=n\frac KN\left(1-\frac KN\right)\frac{N-n}{N-1}.\]

Front: Describe the Categorical distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\) represents one draw from \(m\) categories, with \(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\).

Support
\[\{1,\ldots,m\}\] after choosing a numerical encoding of the categories.

Example/Intuition
One customer chooses exactly one plan: Basic, Pro, or Enterprise.

PMF
\[P(X=i)=p_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\]

CDF
A scalar CDF requires an ordering/encoding of the categories. Under the encoding \(1,\ldots,m\), \[F_X(x)=\sum_{i\le\lfloor x\rfloor}p_i.\]

Expectation
Not intrinsic for unordered categories. Under the encoding \(1,\ldots,m\), \[\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{i=1}^m i\,p_i.\]

Variance
Not intrinsic for unordered categories. Under the encoding \(1,\ldots,m\), \[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^m i^2p_i-\left(\sum_{i=1}^m i\,p_i\right)^2.\]

Front: Describe the Multinomial distribution.
Back:
Definition
\((X_1,\ldots,X_m)\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n;p_1,\ldots,p_m)\) gives the category counts from \(n\) independent categorical trials, where \(\sum_i p_i=1\).

Support
Vectors \((x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) of nonnegative integers satisfying \[\sum_{i=1}^m x_i=n.\]

Example/Intuition
Observe 100 customers and record how many choose Basic, Pro, and Enterprise; the resulting count vector is Multinomial.

PMF
\[P(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_m=x_m)=\frac{n!}{x_1!\cdots x_m!}\prod_{i=1}^m p_i^{x_i}.\]

CDF
The multivariate CDF is \[F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=P(X_1\le x_1,\ldots,X_m\le x_m),\] obtained by summing the joint PMF over feasible count vectors satisfying those bounds.

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X_i]=np_i.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=np_i(1-p_i).\] For \(i\ne j\), \[\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=-np_ip_j.\]

Front: Describe the continuous Uniform distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b)\), \(a
Support
\[[a,b].\]

Example/Intuition
If an arrival is equally likely at any time from 2pm to 3pm, the arrival time is Uniform over that hour.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\begin{cases}\frac1{b-a},&a\le x\le b,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&xb.\end{cases}\]

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac{a+b}{2}.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}.\]

Key property
For every individual \(x\), \(P(X=x)=0\); probability comes from area under the density, not the PDF value itself.

Front: Describe the Normal (Gaussian) distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) models symmetric variation around \(\mu\), often arising approximately from many small additive effects.

Support
\[\mathbb R.\]

Example/Intuition
Repeated measurement errors around a true value are often approximately Normal: most errors are small, with large errors increasingly rare on either side.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\Phi\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right),\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard Normal CDF; it has no elementary closed form.

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\mu.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.\]

Key property
Standardization gives \[Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).\]

Front: Describe the Exponential distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(\lambda)\), \(\lambda>0\), models the waiting time until the next event in a constant-rate Poisson process.

Support
\[[0,\infty).\]

Example/Intuition
If calls arrive randomly at a steady average rate, \(X\) can be the time from now until the next call.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda x},&x\ge0,\\0,&x<0.\end{cases}\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0,\\1-e^{-\lambda x},&x\ge0.\end{cases}\]

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac1\lambda.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac1{\lambda^2}.\]

Key property
Memorylessness: \[P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t).\] It is the continuous waiting-time analogue of the Geometric distribution.

Front: Describe the Gamma distribution.
Back:
Definition
Using the shape-rate parameterization, \(X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda)\), \(\alpha,\lambda>0\), models accumulated positive waiting time; when \(\alpha\) is a positive integer it is the waiting time until the \(\alpha\)-th event in a rate-\(\lambda\) Poisson process, equivalently a sum of \(\alpha\) independent Exponential\((\lambda)\) waiting times.

Support
\[[0,\infty).\]

Example/Intuition
If calls arrive at a steady random rate, the waiting time until the 5th call is Gamma distributed.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x},\qquad x\ge0.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\int_0^x\frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}t^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda t}\,dt\] for \(x\ge0\); generally there is no elementary closed form.

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac{\alpha}{\lambda}.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{\alpha}{\lambda^2}.\]

Connection
\[\operatorname{Gamma}(1,\lambda)=\operatorname{Exponential}(\lambda).\]

Convention
Some sources use scale \(\theta=1/\lambda\) instead of rate; check the parameterization.

Front: Describe the Beta distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\), \(\alpha,\beta>0\), is a flexible model for probabilities and proportions on \([0,1]\).

Support
\[[0,1].\]

Example/Intuition
If the true conversion rate is unknown, a Beta distribution can represent our uncertainty about that probability before or after seeing data.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\frac{x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)},\qquad 0
CDF
\[F_X(x)=\int_0^x\frac{t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}\,dt,\] generally with no elementary closed form.

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}.\]

Key property
\(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)=\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Roughly, \(\alpha>\beta\) shifts mass toward 1, \(\alpha<\beta\) toward 0, and large \(\alpha+\beta\) concentrates the distribution around its mean.

Front: Describe the Chi-squared distribution.
Back:
Definition
If \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), then \[X=Z_1^2+\cdots+Z_k^2\sim\chi_k^2.\] It therefore measures accumulated squared standardized variation and appears naturally in variance estimation and testing.

Support
\[[0,\infty).\]

Example/Intuition
Take several independent standardized Normal errors, square them, and add them; the total squared standardized error is Chi-squared.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\frac{1}{2^{k/2}\Gamma(k/2)}x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2},\qquad x>0.\]

CDF
Obtained by integrating the PDF; there is generally no elementary closed form.

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=k.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=2k.\]

Connection
Under the shape-rate convention, \[\chi_k^2=\operatorname{Gamma}\left(\frac{k}{2},\frac12\right).\]

Front: Describe Student's \(t\) distribution.
Back:
Definition
If \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(V\sim\chi_ u^2\) are independent, then \[T= rac{Z}{\sqrt{V/ u}}\sim t_ u.\] It is Normal-like but has heavier tails, reflecting the extra uncertainty that appears when an unknown scale is estimated from finite data.

Support
\[\mathbb R.\]

Example/Intuition
When estimating a population mean from a small Normal sample with unknown variance, the standardized sample mean follows a \(t\) distribution rather than an exact standard Normal.

PDF
\[f_T(t)= rac{\Gamma(( u+1)/2)}{\sqrt{ u\pi}\,\Gamma( u/2)}\left(1+ rac{t^2}{ u} ight)^{-( u+1)/2}.\]

CDF
Obtained by integrating the PDF; there is generally no elementary closed form.

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[T]=0\quad ext{for } u>1;\] for \( u\le1\), the expectation does not exist.

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(T)= rac{ u}{ u-2}\quad ext{for } u>2.\] It is infinite for \(1< u\le2\) and undefined for \( u\le1\).

Key property
As \( u o\infty\), \(t_ u\) approaches \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).

Front: Describe the \(F\) distribution.
Back:
Definition
If \(U\sim\chi_{d_1}^2\) and \(V\sim\chi_{d_2}^2\) are independent, then \[X=\frac{U/d_1}{V/d_2}\sim F_{d_1,d_2}.\] It is a ratio of independent variance-like quantities, which is why it appears in ANOVA, regression \(F\)-tests, and variance comparisons.

Support
\[(0,\infty).\]

Example/Intuition
ANOVA compares variation explained between groups with unexplained variation within groups; their ratio has an \(F\)-distribution under the null model.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\frac{(d_1/d_2)^{d_1/2}x^{d_1/2-1}}{B(d_1/2,d_2/2)\left(1+(d_1/d_2)x\right)^{(d_1+d_2)/2}},\qquad x>0.\]

CDF
Obtained by integrating the PDF; there is generally no elementary closed form.

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac{d_2}{d_2-2}\quad\text{for }d_2>2;\] otherwise the expectation does not exist.

Variance
For \(d_2>4\), \[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{2d_2^2(d_1+d_2-2)}{d_1(d_2-2)^2(d_2-4)}.\] The variance is not finite when \(d_2\le4\).

Front: Describe the Lognormal distribution.
Back:
Definition
\(X\sim\operatorname{Lognormal}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) means \[\log X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2).\] It is natural for positive quantities generated by multiplicative rather than additive effects and is typically right-skewed.

Support
\[(0,\infty).\]

Example/Intuition
If a quantity grows through many multiplicative percentage effects, such as a size built by repeated proportional growth, its distribution can be approximately Lognormal.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\frac{1}{x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{(\log x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad x>0.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\Phi\left(\frac{\log x-\mu}{\sigma}\right),\qquad x>0.\]

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}.\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\left(e^{\sigma^2}-1\right)e^{2\mu+\sigma^2}.\]

Key property
\(e^\mu\) is the median, not the mean; in particular \(\mathbb E[X]\ne e^\mu\) unless \(\sigma=0\).

Front: Describe the Weibull distribution.
Back:
Definition
Using shape \(k>0\) and scale \(\lambda>0\), \(X\sim\operatorname{Weibull}(k,\lambda)\) is a flexible model for lifetimes and waiting times because its event/failure rate can decrease, remain constant, or increase over time.

Support
\[[0,\infty).\]

Example/Intuition
Let \(X\) be the lifetime of a machine component; Weibull can model whether failure becomes more or less likely as the component ages.

PDF
\[f_X(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^k\right],\qquad x\ge0.\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=1-\exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^k\right],\qquad x\ge0.\]

Expectation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\lambda\Gamma\left(1+\frac1k\right).\]

Variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda^2\left[\Gamma\left(1+\frac2k\right)-\Gamma\left(1+\frac1k\right)^2\right].\]

Key property
\(k<1\) gives decreasing hazard, \(k=1\) constant hazard, and \(k>1\) increasing hazard. In particular, \[\operatorname{Weibull}(1,\lambda)=\operatorname{Exponential}(1/\lambda)\] under this scale parameterization.

Front: Describe the Johnson \(S_U\) distribution.
Back:
Definition
Using parameters \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(\delta>0\), location \(\xi\in\mathbb R\), and scale \(\lambda>0\), \(X\) has a Johnson \(S_U\) distribution when \[Z=\gamma+\delta\operatorname{asinh}\left(\frac{X-\xi}{\lambda}\right)\sim\mathcal N(0,1).\] Equivalently, \(X=\xi+\lambda\sinh((Z-\gamma)/\delta)\). It is a flexible unbounded model for empirical data with skewness and/or heavy tails.

Support
\[\mathbb R.\]

Example/Intuition
If measurement residuals are strongly skewed with unusually heavy tails, Johnson \(S_U\) can flexibly fit that shape by transforming them to Normality.

PDF
Let \(y=(x-\xi)/\lambda\). Then \[f_X(x)=\frac{\delta}{\lambda\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt{1+y^2}}\exp\left[-\frac12\left(\gamma+\delta\operatorname{asinh}(y)\right)^2\right].\]

CDF
\[F_X(x)=\Phi\left(\gamma+\delta\operatorname{asinh}\left(\frac{x-\xi}{\lambda}\right)\right).\]

Expectation
The mean is finite and has a closed form, but it is not a recall target for this card; the Normal-transform definition and interpretation are the durable facts.

Variance
The variance is finite and has a closed form, but it is not a recall target for this card.

Key property
The sinh/asinh transformation lets the family represent a wide range of skewness and tail weights while remaining supported on all of \(\mathbb R\).

Front: What is the joint distribution (joint law) of real-valued random variables \(X,Y\) defined on the same probability space?
Back:
Definition
The map \[(X,Y):\Omega\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad \omega\mapsto(X(\omega),Y(\omega))\] is an \(\mathbb R^2\)-valued random variable. Its joint law is the pushforward probability measure \[P_{(X,Y)}(A):=P\big((X,Y)\in A\big),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2).\]

Interpretation
It describes how \(X\) and \(Y\) behave together, not merely their individual distributions.

Front: What are the marginal distributions of a joint law \(P_{(X,Y)}\)?
Back:
Definition
The marginal laws are the individual laws of \(X\) and \(Y\). For \(A,B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\), \[P_X(A)=P_{(X,Y)}(A\times\mathbb R),\] \[P_Y(B)=P_{(X,Y)}(\mathbb R\times B).\]

Key fact
The joint law determines its marginals, but the marginals generally do not determine the joint law.

Front: What are the joint PMF and joint PDF of two real-valued random variables, and how are the marginals recovered?
Back:
Discrete case
\[p_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y).\] The marginal PMFs are \[p_X(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb R}p_{X,Y}(x,y),\qquad p_Y(y)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb R}p_{X,Y}(x,y),\] where only countably many terms can be nonzero.

Absolutely continuous case
A joint PDF \(f_{X,Y}\) satisfies \[P((X,Y)\in A)=\iint_A f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy.\] The marginal densities are \[f_X(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy,\qquad f_Y(y)=\int_{\mathbb R}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx.\]

Front: How do you compute \(\mathbb E[g(X,Y)]\) from the joint distribution of \(X,Y\)?
Back:
General form
For integrable \(g(X,Y)\), \[\mathbb E[g(X,Y)]=\int_{\mathbb R^2}g(x,y)\,dP_{(X,Y)}(x,y).\]

Discrete
\[\mathbb E[g(X,Y)]=\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2}g(x,y)p_{X,Y}(x,y).\]

Absolutely continuous
\[\mathbb E[g(X,Y)]=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}g(x,y)f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy.\]

Special case
\(\mathbb E[XY]\) is obtained by taking \(g(x,y)=xy\).

Front: What is the covariance of two real-valued random variables \(X,Y\), and what is its equivalent computational formula?
Back:
Definition
For \(X,Y\) with finite second moments, \[\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E\left[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])\right].\]

Equivalent formula
\[\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].\]

Interpretation
Positive covariance means deviations from the two means tend to have the same sign; negative covariance means they tend to have opposite signs.

Connection
\[\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)=\operatorname{Var}(X).\]

Front: What does it mean for real-valued random variables \(X,Y\) to be independent?
Back:
Definition
\(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if for every \(A,B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\), \[P((X,Y)\in A\times B)=P(X\in A)P(Y\in B).\]

Front: How does independence of \(X,Y\) appear in their PMFs, PDFs, and expectations?
Back:
Discrete case
\[X\perp Y\iff p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)\] for all \(x,y\).

Absolutely continuous case
\[X\perp Y\iff f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)\] almost everywhere.

Expectation consequence
If \(X,Y\) are independent, then for suitable integrable functions \(g,h\), \[\mathbb E[g(X)h(Y)]=\mathbb E[g(X)]\mathbb E[h(Y)].\] In particular, \[\mathbb E[XY]=\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y],\] so \[X\perp Y\implies\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.\] The converse is false.

Front: Give a simple example of dependent random variables with zero covariance.
Back:
Example
Let \[X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(-1,1)\] and define \[Y=X^2.\] They are dependent because \(Y\) is completely determined by \(X\).

Covariance
By symmetry, \[\mathbb E[X]=0,\qquad \mathbb E[X^3]=0.\] Hence \[\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[X^3]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[X^2]=0.\]

Conclusion
\[\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0\not\Rightarrow X\perp Y.\]

Front: What is the correlation of \(X,Y\), and what are its fundamental bounds and interpretations?
Back:
Definition
If \(0<\operatorname{Var}(X),\operatorname{Var}(Y)<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\rho_{X,Y}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}.\]

Bound
By Cauchy-Schwarz, \[-1\le\rho_{X,Y}\le1.\]

Interpretation
Correlation is a dimensionless measure of linear association.

Equality case
\(|\rho|=1\) iff \(X\) and \(Y\) have an exact affine relationship \(Y=aX+b\) almost surely, with the sign of \(a\) determining the sign of \(\rho\).

Warning
Zero correlation does not imply independence.

Front: How does covariance transform under affine transformations of \(X\) and \(Y\)?
Back:
Affine transformation
For constants \(a,b,c,d\), \[\operatorname{Cov}(aX+b,cY+d)=ac\,\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).\]

Interpretation
Adding constants does not affect covariance; scaling multiplies covariance by the product of the scale factors.

Consequence
\[\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).\]

Front: Give a simple probability game whose payout has infinite expectation.
Back:
St. Petersburg game
Flip a fair coin until the first heads. If the first heads occurs on flip \(n\), receive \[X=2^n.\] Since \[P(X=2^n)=2^{-n},\] the expected payout is \[\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^n2^{-n}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1=\infty.\]

Interpretation
\(X\) has a perfectly valid probability distribution but \[\mathbb E[X]=\infty.\] Existence of a probability law does not imply a finite expectation.

Front: What is \(\sigma(Y)\) for a real-valued random variable \(Y\), and what does it represent?
Back:
Definition
\[\sigma(Y):=\{Y^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}.\] It is the sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra generated by \(Y\).

Interpretation
\(\sigma(Y)\) represents exactly the distinctions in \(\Omega\) that can be made using \(Y\) alone. In the discrete case, it consists of unions of the level sets \(\{Y=y\}\).

Front: What does it mean for a random variable \(Z\) to be \(\sigma(Y)\)-measurable?
Back:
Definition
\(Z\) is \(\sigma(Y)\)-measurable if \[Z^{-1}(B)\in\sigma(Y)\] for every \(B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\).

Equivalent form
For real-valued random variables, \[Z\text{ is }\sigma(Y)\text{-measurable}\iff Z=g(Y)\] for some Borel-measurable \(g\).

Discrete intuition
\(Z\) must be constant on each level set \(\{Y=y\}\). Thus \(Z\) can depend on \(\omega\) only through \(Y(\omega)\).

Front: For discrete \(Y\), how is \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\) defined as a random variable?
Back:
Definition
For discrete \(Y\), assuming the relevant conditional expectations exist, \[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]:\Omega\to\mathbb R\] is given by \[\boxed{\omega\mapsto \mathbb E[X\mid Y=Y(\omega)]}.\]

Interpretation
On the level set \(\{Y=y\}\), the random variable \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\) is constant with value \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]\).

Front: What is the general definition of \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\)?
Back:
Definition
Let \(X\in L^1\) and let \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) be a sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra. A conditional expectation of \(X\) given \(\mathcal G\) is an integrable random variable \(Z\) such that \[Z\text{ is }\mathcal G\text{-measurable}\] and \[\int_A Z\,dP=\int_A X\,dP\qquad\forall A\in\mathcal G.\]

Existence and uniqueness
Such a \(Z\) exists and is unique up to equality almost surely, and is denoted \[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G].\]

Conditioning on a random variable
\[\boxed{\mathbb E[X\mid Y]:=\mathbb E[X\mid\sigma(Y)]}.\]

Front: How do you compute the conditional law of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) in the discrete and absolutely continuous cases?
Back:
Discrete
For \(P(Y=y)>0\), \[p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}.\] Then \[\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]=\sum_x x\,p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y).\]

Absolutely continuous
For \(f_Y(y)>0\), \[f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},\] and \[\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]=\int_{\mathbb R}x f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx.\] For continuous \(Y\), this is not ordinary event conditioning on \(\{Y=y\}\), since typically \(P(Y=y)=0\).

Front: What is the law of total expectation?
Back:
Statement
For integrable \(X\), \[\boxed{\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]=\mathbb E[X]}.\]

Discrete form
\[\boxed{\mathbb E[X]=\sum_y \mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]P(Y=y)}.\]

Interpretation
Averaging the conditional means over the distribution of \(Y\) recovers the overall mean.

Front: What can be pulled out of a conditional expectation?
Back:
Statement
If \(Z\) is \(\sigma(Y)\)-measurable and the required integrability conditions hold, then \[\boxed{\mathbb E[ZX\mid Y]=Z\,\mathbb E[X\mid Y]}.\]

Special cases
\[\mathbb E[h(Y)X\mid Y]=h(Y)\mathbb E[X\mid Y],\qquad \mathbb E[h(Y)\mid Y]=h(Y).\]

Interpretation
Conditioning on \(Y\) does not average quantities already determined by \(Y\).

Front: What is the tower property of conditional expectation?
Back:
Statement
If \[\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\] and \(X\in L^1\), then \[\boxed{\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal H]}.\]

Common form
\[\boxed{\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y,Z]\mid Y]=\mathbb E[X\mid Y]}.\]

Interpretation
Condition on finer information and then reduce to coarser information; the result is the same as conditioning on the coarser information directly.

Front: If \(X\) is independent of \(Y\), what is \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\)?
Back:
Statement
If \(X\in L^1\) and \(X\) is independent of \(Y\), then \[\boxed{\mathbb E[X\mid Y]=\mathbb E[X]\quad\text{a.s.}}\] The right-hand side is the constant random variable \(\omega\mapsto\mathbb E[X]\).

Interpretation
\(Y\) provides no information that changes the mean of \(X\).

Front: What is the conditional variance of \(X\) given \(Y\)?
Back:
Definition
For square-integrable \(X\), \[\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2\mid Y]}.\]

Equivalent form
\[\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)=\mathbb E[X^2\mid Y]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]^2}.\]

Interpretation
Conditional variance measures the variation in \(X\) remaining after conditioning on \(Y\).

Front: What is the law of total variance, and how should it be interpreted?
Back:
Statement
\[\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]+\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[X\mid Y])}.\]

Interpretation
\[\text{total variation}=\text{average within-}Y\text{ variation}+\text{between-}Y\text{ variation}.\] The first term is the average variance remaining after \(Y\) is known. The second measures how much the conditional mean changes with \(Y\).

Front: Why is conditional expectation fundamental for squared-error regression?
Back:
Statement
For \(X\in L^2\), \[\boxed{\mathbb E[X\mid Y]=\arg\min_{Z\in L^2,\;Z\ \sigma(Y)\text{-measurable}}\mathbb E[(X-Z)^2]}.\]

Decomposition
For every such \(Z\), \[\mathbb E[(X-Z)^2]=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2]+\mathbb E[(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]-Z)^2].\]

Interpretation
Among all square-integrable predictors that can use only \(Y\), the conditional mean is the \(L^2\)-optimal predictor of \(X\): it minimizes population mean squared error.

Front: What does it mean for a sequence of random variables \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) to be mutually independent?
Back:
Definition
A sequence \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) is mutually independent if, for every finite set of distinct indices \(i_1,\ldots,i_k\) and every \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\), \[P(X_{i_1}\in A_1,\ldots,X_{i_k}\in A_k)=\prod_{j=1}^kP(X_{i_j}\in A_j).\]

Key distinction
Mutual independence is stronger than pairwise independence: the factorisation must hold for every finite subcollection, not just every pair.

Front: What does it mean for random variables \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) to be i.i.d.?
Back:
Definition
Random variables \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) on a common probability space are i.i.d. when they are both:
1. mutually independent; and
2. identically distributed, so \[P_{X_i}=P_{X_j}\qquad\forall i,j.\]

Equivalent form
Identical distribution means \[P(X_i\in A)=P(X_j\in A)\] for every \(A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\) and every \(i,j\).

Front: What does \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}X\) mean?
Back:
Definition
\[X_n\xrightarrow{P}X\] means \[\forall\varepsilon>0,\ \forall\eta>0,\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\] such that \[n\ge N\implies P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)<\eta.\]

Equivalent form
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\to0.\]

Front: What does \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}X\) mean?
Back:
Definition
\[X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}X\] means \[P\left(\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\}\right)=1.\]

Equivalent pathwise form
With probability \(1\), \[\forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists N=N(\omega,\varepsilon)\] such that \[n\ge N\implies |X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|<\varepsilon.\]

Interpretation
For almost every fixed \(\omega\), the numerical sequence \(X_n(\omega)\) converges to \(X(\omega)\).

Front: What is the relationship between almost sure convergence and convergence in probability?
Back:
Statement
\[\boxed{X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}X\implies X_n\xrightarrow{P}X.}\] The converse is false in general.

Key distinction
Almost sure convergence controls the entire infinite trajectory for almost every \(\omega\); convergence in probability only says that the probability of a large error at time \(n\) tends to zero.

Front: State the Weak Law of Large Numbers for i.i.d. random variables.
Back:
Statement
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. real-valued random variables with \[\mathbb E[|X_1|]<\infty,\qquad \mu=\mathbb E[X_1],\] and define \[\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.\] Then \[\boxed{\bar X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu.}\]

Interpretation
For every fixed error tolerance, the probability that the sample average lies outside that tolerance tends to \(0\).

Front: State the Strong Law of Large Numbers for i.i.d. random variables.
Back:
Statement
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. real-valued random variables with \[\mathbb E[|X_1|]<\infty,\qquad \mu=\mathbb E[X_1].\] Then \[\boxed{\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mu.}\]

Equivalent pathwise form
\[P\left(\left\{\omega:\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i(\omega)\to\mu\right\}\right)=1.\]

Interpretation
With probability \(1\), one realised infinite sequence has a running average converging to \(\mu\).

Front: What does \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) mean?
Back:
Definition
Let \[F_{X_n}(x)=P(X_n\le x),\qquad F_X(x)=P(X\le x).\] Then \[X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\] means that, for every \(x\) at which \(F_X\) is continuous, \[F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x).\]

Equivalent \(\varepsilon\)-form
For every such \(x\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(N\) such that \[n\ge N\implies \left|P(X_n\le x)-P(X\le x)\right|<\varepsilon.\]

Interpretation
This describes convergence of the distributions, not necessarily convergence of realised values.

Front: Why does convergence in distribution require CDF convergence only at continuity points of the limiting CDF?
Back:
Setup
Let \[X_n=\frac1n\quad\text{a.s.},\qquad X=0\quad\text{a.s.}\] Then \(X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\) for every \(\omega\).

At the jump
\[F_{X_n}(0)=P(X_n\le0)=0\] for every \(n\), while \[F_X(0)=P(X\le0)=1.\] Thus \(F_{X_n}(0)\not\to F_X(0)\).

Away from the jump
For \(x<0\), both CDFs equal \(0\). For every fixed \(x>0\), eventually \(1/n\le x\), so both CDFs equal \(1\).

Conclusion
The failure occurs only at \(0\), where \(F_X\) jumps. Requiring convergence at jumps would reject this natural convergence, which is why convergence in distribution only requires CDF convergence at continuity points of the limit.

Front: State the classical Central Limit Theorem for i.i.d. random variables.
Back:
Statement
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. real-valued random variables with \[\mathbb E[X_i]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2,\qquad 0<\sigma^2<\infty.\] Define \[\overline X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.\] Then \[\boxed{\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)}.\]

Equivalent CDF form
For every \(x\in\mathbb R\), \[P\left(\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}\le x\right)\to\Phi(x),\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard Normal CDF.

Interpretation
After centring the sample mean and scaling its fluctuations to order \(1\), the distribution approaches the standard Normal.

Front: For i.i.d. random variables with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2<\infty\), what are the mean, variance, and standard deviation of the sample mean?
Back:
Setup
For \[\overline X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\] with i.i.d. variables having mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2<\infty\):

Mean, variance, and SD
\[\mathbb E[\overline X_n]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\overline X_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\qquad \operatorname{SD}(\overline X_n)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.\]

Standardization
Therefore, \[\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}=\frac{\overline X_n-\mathbb E[\overline X_n]}{\operatorname{SD}(\overline X_n)}.\] This normalized variable has mean \(0\) and variance \(1\) for every \(n\).

Connection to the CLT
The CLT additionally says that the distribution of this normalized variable converges to \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).

Front: What is the distribution of a linear combination of independent Normal random variables?
Back:
Statement
If \(X_i\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)\) independently, then \[\sum_i a_iX_i\sim N\left(\sum_i a_i\mu_i,\,\sum_i a_i^2\sigma_i^2\right).\]

Special case
If \(X_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \[\bar X_n\sim N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\] exactly, for every \(n\).

Front: Informally, what do the Law of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem say about sample averages?
Back:
Informal interpretation only

Law of Large Numbers
As more i.i.d. observations are averaged, the sample average settles near the population mean \(\mu\). The LLN says the unscaled error \(\overline X_n-\mu\) disappears.

Central Limit Theorem
The remaining sample-mean fluctuations occur on the scale \(1/\sqrt n\). After centring the sample mean, magnifying by \(\sqrt n\), and scaling by \(\sigma\), the distribution of those fluctuations approaches the standard Normal distribution.

The observations themselves do not become Normal. The Normal limit describes the distribution of repeated normalized sample averages.

Front: If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, how is the distribution of \(X+Y\) obtained?
Back:
Statement
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, the distribution of \(X+Y\) is obtained by convolution.

Discrete case
\[p_{X+Y}(s)=\sum_x p_X(x)p_Y(s-x).\]

Continuous case
\[f_{X+Y}(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_X(x)f_Y(s-x)\,dx.\]

Role of independence
Independence is what allows the joint distribution to factor into the two marginals.

Front: For \(S=\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\), what are \(\mathbb E[S]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S)\)?
Back:
Expectation
Always, \[\mathbb E[S]=\sum_i a_i\mathbb E[X_i].\]

Variance
In general, \[\operatorname{Var}(S)=\sum_i a_i^2\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{i
If the \(X_i\) are independent, \[\operatorname{Var}(S)=\sum_i a_i^2\operatorname{Var}(X_i).\]

Front: What important distribution families are closed under independent sums?
Back:
Statement
Important distribution families are closed under independent sums:
\[\operatorname{Bin}(n_1,p)+\operatorname{Bin}(n_2,p)\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n_1+n_2,p),\] \[\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1)+\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_2)\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2),\] for a common rate \(\beta\), \[\Gamma(\alpha_1,\beta)+\Gamma(\alpha_2,\beta)\sim\Gamma(\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\beta),\] and \[\chi^2_{k_1}+\chi^2_{k_2}\sim\chi^2_{k_1+k_2}.\]

Condition
All sums above assume independence.
Tags: probability sums closure binomial poisson gamma chi-squared

Front: How is the chi-squared distribution related to independent standard Normal random variables?
Back:
Statement
If \[Z_1,\dots,Z_n\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1),\] then \[\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2\sim\chi_n^2.\]

Equivalent standardized form
If \(X_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \[\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2\sim\chi_n^2.\]

Front: What is a statistical model?
Back:
Definition
A statistical model is a family \[\mathcal P=\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\] of probability measures on a common measurable sample space \((\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\).

Parameter
\(\Theta\) is the parameter space; observed data \(X\) have law \(P_\theta\) for an unknown \(\theta\in\Theta\).

Front: What is the joint law of an i.i.d. sample in a statistical model?
Back:
Definition
If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent with common law \(Q_\theta\), their joint law on the product sample space is \[P_\theta=Q_\theta^{\otimes n}.\]

Front: What makes a statistical model identifiable?
Back:
Definition
The parametrization is identifiable if \(P_\theta=P_{\theta'}\) implies \(\theta=\theta'\).

Target identifiability
A target \(\psi(\theta)\) is identifiable if \(P_\theta=P_{\theta'}\) implies \(\psi(\theta)=\psi(\theta')\).

Front: What is an estimand?
Back:
Definition
An estimand is a fixed unknown target \(\psi(\theta)\), where \(\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R^k\) specifies the feature of the data law to be estimated.

Example
The target may be \(\theta\) itself, a mean, a variance, or a probability under \(P_\theta\).

Front: What is a statistic?
Back:
Definition
A statistic is a measurable function \(T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal T\) of the sample, not depending on any unknown parameter.

Examples
Sample mean, sample variance, sample maximum, and category counts.

Front: What is an estimator of an estimand?
Back:
Definition
An estimator \(T_n:\mathcal X_n\to\mathbb R^k\) is a statistic used to estimate \(\psi(\theta)\).

Distinction
Before sampling \(T_n(X)\) is random; after observing \(X=x\), its value \(T_n(x)\) is a fixed estimate.

Front: What is the sampling distribution of an estimator?
Back:
Definition
For \(X\sim P_\theta\) and statistic \(T_n\), the sampling law is \(P_\theta\circ T_n^{-1}\), meaning \[(P_\theta\circ T_n^{-1})(B)=P_\theta(T_n(X)\in B).\]

Front: Define the bias of a real-valued estimator.
Back:
Definition
For integrable estimator \(T_n\) of \(\psi(\theta)\), \[\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T_n)=\mathbb E_\theta[T_n]-\psi(\theta).\]

Unbiasedness
It is unbiased if \(\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T_n)=0\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).

Front: Define the variance of a real-valued estimator.
Back:
Definition
For an estimator with finite second moment, \[\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T_n)=\mathbb E_\theta[(T_n-\mathbb E_\theta[T_n])^2].\]

Front: Define the mean squared error (MSE) of an estimator.
Back:
Definition
For a scalar target \(\psi(\theta)\), \[\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T_n)=\mathbb E_\theta[(T_n-\psi(\theta))^2],\] when the expectation exists.

Front: State and derive the bias-variance decomposition.
Back:
Statement
\[\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)+\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)^2.\]

Derivation
Expand \(T-\psi=(T-\mathbb E_\theta T)+(\mathbb E_\theta T-\psi)\) and take expectations. The cross term vanishes.

Front: What does consistency of an estimator mean?
Back:
Definition
An estimator sequence \(T_n\) of \(\psi(\theta)\) is consistent if for each fixed \(\theta\in\Theta\) and each \(\varepsilon>0\), \[P_\theta(|T_n-\psi(\theta)|>\varepsilon)\to0.\]

Equivalent form
\(T_n\xrightarrow{P_\theta}\psi(\theta)\).

Front: Prove that vanishing MSE implies consistency.
Back:
Condition
Assume \(\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T_n)\to0\) for every fixed \(\theta\).

Proof
For \(\varepsilon>0\), Markov's inequality yields \[P_\theta(|T_n-\psi(\theta)|>\varepsilon)\le\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T_n)/\varepsilon^2\to0.\]

Front: What is the standard error of a statistic?
Back:
Definition
\[\operatorname{SE}_\theta(T_n)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T_n)}.\]

Special case
For i.i.d. observations with variance \(\sigma^2\), \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X_n)=\sigma/\sqrt n\), whereas each observation has standard deviation \(\sigma\).

Front: What is a consistent estimator of standard error?
Back:
Definition
For nonzero true standard error \(s_n(\theta)\), a data-based \(\hat s_n\) is relatively consistent if \[\hat s_n/s_n(\theta)\xrightarrow{P_\theta}1.\]

Example
For i.i.d. finite-variance data with \(\sigma>0\), \(S_n/\sqrt n\) is relatively consistent for \(\sigma/\sqrt n\).

Front: Define the sample variance and state its expectation.
Back:
Definition
For \(n\ge2\), \[S_n^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2.\]

Statement
For i.i.d. data with finite variance \(\sigma^2\), \(\mathbb E[S_n^2]=\sigma^2\). The denominator-\(n\) version has expectation \((n-1)\sigma^2/n\).

Front: Give a biased estimator with smaller MSE than an unbiased estimator.
Back:
Setup
For \(X\sim N(\theta,1)\), compare \(T_1=X\) and \(T_2=X/2\).

Calculation
\[\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T_1)=1,\quad \operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T_2)=(1+\theta^2)/4.\]

Conclusion
The biased \(T_2\) has smaller MSE for \(|\theta|<\sqrt 3\).

Front: Define a population raw moment and a sample raw moment.
Back:
Population
The \(j\)-th raw moment (when it exists) is \(m_j(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[X_1^j]\).

Sample
The \(j\)-th sample raw moment is \(\hat m_j=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^j\).

Front: How is a method of moments estimator constructed?
Back:
Definition
For a \(k\)-parameter i.i.d. model, select \(k\) moments \(m_j(\theta)\) and solve \[m_j(\hat\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^j,\quad j=1,\ldots,k.\]

Warning
An admissible solution may fail to exist or may not be unique.

Front: Find the method of moments estimator for Bernoulli data.
Back:
Setup
If \(X_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), then \(\mathbb E_p[X_i]=p\).

Answer
Equating the first moments yields \(\hat p_{\rm MM}=\bar X_n\).

Front: Find the method of moments estimator for Poisson data.
Back:
Setup
If \(X_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), then \(\mathbb E_\lambda[X_i]=\lambda\).

Answer
\[\hat\lambda_{\rm MM}=\bar X_n.\]

Front: Find the method of moments estimators of the Normal mean and variance.
Back:
Setup
For \(X_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(\mathbb E[X_i]=\mu\) and \(\mathbb E[X_i^2]=\mu^2+\sigma^2\).

Answer
\[\hat\mu_{\rm MM}=\bar X_n,\quad\widehat{\sigma^2}_{\rm MM}=\frac1n\sum_i X_i^2-\bar X_n^2.\]

Front: What is the likelihood function for observed data?
Back:
Definition
For a model with densities or PMFs \(p_\theta\) relative to a common dominating measure, the likelihood is \[L_x(\theta)=p_\theta(x),\qquad\theta\in\Theta.\]

Distinction
The observed \(x\) is held fixed; \(L_x(\theta)\) is not a probability distribution over \(\theta\).

Front: What is the likelihood of an i.i.d. sample?
Back:
Formula
For independent \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) with common density or mass function \(f_\theta\), \[L_x(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n f_\theta(x_i).\]

Front: Define the log-likelihood and its relation to likelihood maximization.
Back:
Definition
\[\ell_x(\theta)=\log L_x(\theta)\] where \(L_x(\theta)>0\). For an i.i.d. sample, \(\ell_x(\theta)=\sum_i\log f_\theta(x_i)\).

Equivalence
Since \(\log\) is strictly increasing, the likelihood and log-likelihood have the same maximizers on their common domain.

Front: What is a maximum likelihood estimator (MLE)?
Back:
Definition
An MLE \(\hat\theta(X)\) is a statistic for which \[L_x(\hat\theta(x))=\max_{\theta\in\Theta}L_x(\theta),\] where the maximum exists and a measurable maximizer can be selected.

Warning
A maximum need not exist or be unique.

Front: What is the score equation for a differentiable log-likelihood?
Back:
Definition
For scalar \(\theta\), the score is \(U_x(\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ell_x(\theta)\).

Necessary condition
An interior differentiable local maximum satisfies \(U_x(\hat\theta)=0\), but stationary points need not be global maxima and boundary solutions must be checked.

Front: Derive the MLE for a Bernoulli parameter.
Back:
Setup
For i.i.d. Bernoulli observations, put \(s=\sum_i x_i\). Then \[L_x(p)=p^s(1-p)^{n-s},\quad 0\le p\le1.\]

Answer
\[\hat p_{\rm MLE}=s/n=\bar X_n,\] including the endpoint cases \(s=0,n\).

Front: Derive the MLE for the parameter of a Poisson sample.
Back:
Setup
For i.i.d. Poisson observations, \[\ell_x(\lambda)=-n\lambda+\Big(\sum_i x_i\Big)\log\lambda-\sum_i\log(x_i!).\]

Answer
\(\hat\lambda=\bar X_n\) if \(\lambda\ge0\). If \(\lambda>0\) and \(\bar X_n=0\), the likelihood has no maximizer in the parameter space.

Front: What is the MLE of a Normal mean when the variance is known?
Back:
Setup
For i.i.d. \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with known \(\sigma^2>0\), \(\ell_x(\mu)=C-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\).

Answer
\[\hat\mu_{\rm MLE}=\bar X_n.\]

Front: What are the MLEs of the mean and variance of a Normal sample?
Back:
Statement
For a nonconstant observed i.i.d. Normal sample with unknown \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2>0\), \[\hat\mu=\bar X_n,\qquad \widehat{\sigma^2}=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)^2.\]

Warning
The variance MLE differs from unbiased \(S_n^2\). If all observations coincide, no maximum exists over \(\sigma^2>0\).

Front: State the equivariance property of the MLE.
Back:
Statement
If \(\hat\theta\) maximizes the likelihood of \(\theta\), then \(g(\hat\theta)\) is an MLE of \(\eta=g(\theta)\), using the induced likelihood \(\sup_{\theta:g(\theta)=\eta}L_x(\theta)\).

Note
No injectivity of \(g\) is required for the conclusion.

Front: What is the exact sampling distribution of the Normal sample variance?
Back:
Statement
For i.i.d. \(X_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(n\ge2\), \[\frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.\]

Property
\(\bar X_n\) and \(S_n^2\) are independent.

Front: How is Student's t distribution defined?
Back:
Definition
If \(Z\sim N(0,1)\) and \(V\sim\chi^2_ u\) are independent, then \[Z/\sqrt{V/ u}\sim t_ u.\]

Front: State the exact Student's t result for a standardized Normal sample mean.
Back:
Statement
For i.i.d. \(X_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), unknown \(\sigma>0\), \(n\ge2\), \[\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{S_n/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.\]

Front: State the central limit theorem for the i.i.d. sample mean.
Back:
Statement
If \(X_i\) are i.i.d. with mean \(\mu\) and \(0<\sigma^2<\infty\), then \[\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).\]

Front: What is asymptotic Normality of an estimator at rate square-root n?
Back:
Definition
For each fixed \(\theta\), \[\sqrt n(T_n-\psi(\theta))\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\tau^2(\theta))\] for some \(0<\tau^2(\theta)<\infty\).

Consequence
The sampling error has approximate scale \(\tau(\theta)/\sqrt n\).

Front: Why are estimators centered and scaled in asymptotic theory?
Back:
Purpose
One studies \(a_n(T_n-\psi(\theta))\) so that the limiting law may be nondegenerate even when \(T_n\xrightarrow{P_\theta}\psi(\theta)\).

Example
The CLT uses \(a_n=\sqrt n\) for a finite-variance sample mean.

Front: State Slutsky's theorem.
Back:
Statement
If \(Y_n\xrightarrow{d}Y\) and \(Z_n\xrightarrow{P}c\), then \(Y_nZ_n\xrightarrow{d}cY\), \(Y_n+Z_n\xrightarrow{d}Y+c\), and, for \(c\ne0\), \(Y_n/Z_n\xrightarrow{d}Y/c\).

Front: How does an estimated asymptotic scale yield an approximate Normal pivot?
Back:
Assumptions
Suppose \(\sqrt n(T_n-\psi(\theta))/\tau(\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)\) and \(\hat\tau_n/\tau(\theta)\xrightarrow{P_\theta}1\).

Result
By Slutsky, \[\frac{T_n-\psi(\theta)}{\hat\tau_n/\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).\]

Front: What is a frequentist confidence set of level 1 minus alpha?
Back:
Definition
For a target \(\psi(\theta)\), a data-dependent set \(C(X)\) is a \((1-\alpha)\) confidence set if \[P_\theta(\psi(\theta)\in C(X))\ge1-\alpha\quad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.\]

Special case
A confidence interval is \(C(X)=[L(X),U(X)]\).

Front: How does inverting a pivotal quantity construct a confidence set?
Back:
Setup
Suppose \(Q(X,\theta)\) has a parameter-free distribution and \(P_\theta(a\le Q(X,\theta)\le b)=1-\alpha\).

Construction
Let \(C(x)=\{\theta:a\le Q(x,\theta)\le b\}\). Then \(P_\theta(\theta\in C(X))=1-\alpha\).

Front: State the exact Normal confidence interval for a mean with known variance.
Back:
Conditions
If \(X_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) independently and \(\sigma>0\) is known, \((\bar X_n-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)\sim N(0,1)\).

Formula
\[\bar X_n\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\] has exact coverage \(1-\alpha\).

Front: State the exact Student's t confidence interval for a Normal mean.
Back:
Conditions
For independent \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) observations with unknown \(\sigma>0\), \(n\ge2\),

Formula
\[\bar X_n\pm t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}\] has exact coverage \(1-\alpha\).

Front: Why is a t quantile used in an exact interval with unknown Normal variance?
Back:
Reason
Replacing unknown \(\sigma\) by random \(S_n\) yields \((\bar X_n-\mu)/(S_n/\sqrt n)\sim t_{n-1}\), not \(N(0,1)\).

Limit
As \(\nu\to\infty\), \(t_\nu\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)\).

Front: Construct an asymptotic Normal confidence interval.
Back:
Assumptions
Suppose \(\sqrt n(T_n-\psi(\theta))/\tau(\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)\) with \(\hat\tau_n/\tau(\theta)\xrightarrow{P_\theta}1\).

Formula
An asymptotic \(1-\alpha\) interval is \[T_n\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\hat\tau_n}{\sqrt n}.\]

Coverage
Its coverage tends to \(1-\alpha\) at each fixed \(\theta\) satisfying the assumptions.

Front: What probability does a frequentist confidence-interval guarantee describe?
Back:
Statement
For fixed \(\theta\), the random interval \(C(X)\) covers \(\psi(\theta)\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\) over repeated draws \(X\sim P_\theta\).

Distinction
After data are observed, \(C(x)\) is fixed; this is not a posterior probability for the fixed unknown parameter.

Front: What is the empirical distribution of a sample?
Back:
Definition
For \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the empirical measure is \(\hat P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i}\). Its CDF is \[\hat F_n(t)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{x_i\le t\}}.\]

Front: State the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem.
Back:
Statement
For i.i.d. observations with common CDF \(F\), \[\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|\hat F_n(t)-F(t)|\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}0.\]

Conditions
No density or moment assumption is needed.

Front: What is a plug-in estimator of a statistical functional?
Back:
Definition
If the target is a functional \(T(F)\) of the population CDF \(F\), the empirical plug-in estimate is \(T(\hat F_n)\).

Example
For the mean functional \(T(F)=\int x\,dF(x)\), the plug-in estimate is the sample mean.

Front: How is an ordinary nonparametric bootstrap sample generated?
Back:
Definition
Conditional on observed i.i.d. data \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), draw \(X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*\) independently from the empirical measure \(\hat P_n\).

Equivalent form
Sample \(n\) indices independently, uniformly, and with replacement from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

Front: What is a bootstrap sampling distribution?
Back:
Definition
Conditional on the data \(X=x\), recompute \(T_n^*=T_n(X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*)\) from bootstrap samples. Its conditional law \(\mathcal L(T_n^*\mid X=x)\) is the bootstrap distribution.

Centered form
For sampling-error approximation, study the conditional law of \(T_n^*-T_n(x)\).

Front: State the bootstrap principle for estimating sampling error.
Back:
Statement
Approximate the unknown sampling distribution of \(T_n-\psi(\theta)\) by the conditional bootstrap distribution of \(T_n^*-T_n(x)\) when the approximation is valid.

Warning
Bootstrap validity requires an appropriate sampling scheme and sufficient regularity of the statistic.

Front: What is the bootstrap estimate of standard error?
Back:
Formula
For \(B\ge2\) bootstrap replicates \(T_1^*,\ldots,T_B^*\), let \(\bar T^*=B^{-1}\sum_b T_b^*\). Then \[\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_{\rm boot}=\sqrt{\frac1{B-1}\sum_b(T_b^*-\bar T^*)^2}.\]

Front: Distinguish bootstrap statistical approximation and Monte Carlo approximation.
Back:
Statistical
Replacing the unknown data law by the empirical law approximates sampling behavior, even if the bootstrap law could be evaluated exactly.

Computational
Using only \(B\) bootstrap draws approximates that conditional law numerically; increasing \(B\) reduces simulation error but cannot repair bootstrap invalidity.

Front: What is the Normal bootstrap confidence interval?
Back:
Formula
If \(T_n\) has an approximately Normal sampling distribution and a valid bootstrap standard error, use \[T_n(x)\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_{\rm boot}.\]

Distinction
Bootstrap estimates scale; Normality still supplies the critical quantile.

Front: How is the basic (pivotal-error) bootstrap interval constructed?
Back:
Setup
Let \(q_p^*\) denote the \(p\)-quantile of centered bootstrap error \(T_n^*-T_n(x)\).

Formula
The \(1-\alpha\) interval is \[[T_n(x)-q_{1-\alpha/2}^*,\ T_n(x)-q_{\alpha/2}^*].\]

Front: What is the percentile bootstrap confidence interval?
Back:
Definition
Let \(r_p^*\) be the \(p\)-quantile of raw bootstrap estimates \(T_n^*\). The percentile interval is \[[r_{\alpha/2}^*,r_{1-\alpha/2}^*].\]

Contrast
The basic interval inverts centered error quantiles, whereas the percentile interval uses raw quantiles directly.

Front: Define the jackknife variance estimator.
Back:
Definition
Let \(T_{(-i)}\) be the statistic recomputed without observation \(i\), and \(\bar T_{(-\cdot)}=n^{-1}\sum_iT_{(-i)}\). Then \[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\rm jack}(T_n)=\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_i(T_{(-i)}-\bar T_{(-\cdot)})^2.\]

Special case
For a sample mean, the jackknife standard error equals \(S_n/\sqrt n\).

Front: How are null and alternative hypotheses defined?
Back:
Definition
Partition the parameter space \(\Theta=\Theta_0\sqcup\Theta_1\). Write \[H_0:\theta\in\Theta_0,\qquad H_1:\theta\in\Theta_1.\]

Front: What are simple and composite hypotheses?
Back:
Simple
A hypothesis is simple if it specifies exactly one distinct probability distribution in \(\mathcal P\).

Composite
It is composite if it allows more than one distinct distribution. Either \(H_0\) or \(H_1\) can be simple or composite.

Front: What is a nonrandomized statistical hypothesis test?
Back:
Definition
It is a measurable decision rule \(\varphi:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}\). Reject \(H_0\) when \(\varphi(X)=1\); otherwise do not reject.

Rejection region
Equivalently choose measurable \(R\subseteq\mathcal X\) and let \(\varphi=\mathbf1_R\).

Front: How does a test statistic determine a rejection region?
Back:
Construction
For measurable \(T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal T\) and measurable \(B\subseteq\mathcal T\), \[R=T^{-1}(B)=\{x:T(x)\in B\}.\]

Special case
An upper-tail rule uses \(B=[c,\infty)\), giving \(R=\{x:T(x)\ge c\}\).

Front: What is the power function of a test?
Back:
Definition
For rejection region \(R\), \[\beta_R(\theta)=P_\theta(X\in R).\]

Interpretation
On \(\Theta_0\) this is Type I rejection probability; on \(\Theta_1\) it is the probability of rejecting a false null.

Front: Define Type I and Type II errors.
Back:
Type I
Reject \(H_0\) when \(\theta\in\Theta_0\); its probability is \(\beta_R(\theta)\).

Type II
Do not reject \(H_0\) when \(\theta\in\Theta_1\); its probability is \(1-\beta_R(\theta)\).

Front: Define a test's size and level.
Back:
Size
\[\operatorname{size}(R)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta_R(\theta).\]

Level
A test has level \(\alpha\) when \(\operatorname{size}(R)\le\alpha\). Size is the actual worst-case null rejection probability; level is an upper bound.

Front: What error-control condition defines a level alpha rejection region?
Back:
Condition
For measurable \(R\subseteq\mathcal X\), \[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}P_\theta(X\in R)\le\alpha.\]

Front: How do you calibrate a critical value for an upper-tail test?
Back:
Construction
For \(R_c=\{x:T(x)\ge c\}\), choose \(c\) with \[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}P_\theta(T(X)\ge c)\le\alpha.\]

Discrete case
The achieved size may be strictly below \(\alpha\) because a threshold giving equality need not exist.

Front: How does enlargement of a rejection region affect power?
Back:
Statement
If \(R_1\subseteq R_2\), then \[\beta_{R_1}(\theta)\le\beta_{R_2}(\theta)\quad\text{for every }\theta.\]

Consequence
Increasing the rejection region raises or maintains both power under alternatives and rejection probabilities under the null.

Front: What is a p-value defined by nested level tests?
Back:
Definition
For a nested family of level-\(\alpha\) rejection sets \(R_\alpha\), \[p(x)=\inf\{\alpha\in(0,1]:x\in R_\alpha\},\] with \(p(x)=1\) if the set is empty.

Interpretation
The infimum significance level at which the observed sample is rejected.

Front: How is a p-value computed from an upper-tail null distribution?
Back:
Definition
If large values of \(T\) count against \(H_0\), a conservative composite-null p-value is \[p(x)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}P_\theta(T(X)\ge T(x)).\]

Simple null
For a simple null the supremum is the single null tail probability.

Front: What property makes a p-value valid under a null hypothesis?
Back:
Definition
A valid p-value is super-uniform under the null: \[P_\theta(p(X)\le u)\le u,\quad 0\le u\le1,\ \theta\in\Theta_0.\]

Consequence
Rejecting when \(p(X)\le\alpha\) controls Type I error at level \(\alpha\).

Front: Why does a p-value depend on the chosen test statistic and rejection direction?
Back:
Reason
The definition of data at least as extreme as observed is determined by the rejection rule, for example \(T\ge c\) versus \(|T|\ge c\).

Consequence
The same data and null hypothesis may yield different p-values for different prespecified tests.

Front: How are confidence sets obtained by inverting hypothesis tests?
Back:
Construction
For each point null \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\), let \(R_{\theta_0}\) be a level-\(\alpha\) rejection region. Define \[C(x)=\{\theta_0:x\notin R_{\theta_0}\}.\]

Coverage
Then \(P_\theta(\theta\in C(X))\ge1-\alpha\) for each \(\theta\).

Front: What does failure to reject a null hypothesis establish?
Back:
Formal statement
It establishes that \(x\notin R\), where \(R\) is the selected rejection region.

Distinction
It does not establish \(\theta\in\Theta_0\); under alternatives, Type II error may occur.

Front: How can a one-sided fair-coin test be calibrated exactly?
Back:
Setup
Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\), \(H_0:p=1/2\), \(H_1:p>1/2\).

Construction
Choose integer \(c\) such that \[P_{1/2}(X\ge c)=\sum_{k=c}^n{n\choose k}2^{-n}\le\alpha;\] reject exactly when \(X\ge c\).

Front: What is the power function of a one-sided Binomial rejection rule?
Back:
Setup
For \(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\) and \(R=\{X\ge c\}\),

Formula
\[\beta(p)=P_p(X\ge c)=\sum_{k=c}^n{n\choose k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.\]
